name: Berkelium

discovery.discoverer: Glenn T. Seaborg and team, University of California, Berkeley

occurrence: Does not occur naturally; produced artificially in particle accelerators/reactors in gram-scale or smaller quantities.
majorUses: No practical applications — used exclusively in nuclear physics research, including as a target material to synthesize even heavier superheavy elements like tennessine
safetyNotes: Intensely radioactive; only ever produced and studied in minute quantities under strict laboratory controls.
notableCharacteristics: Named after Berkeley, California, home of the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory where it and several other transuranium elements were first synthesized.
ncertRelevance: named after a research institution's home city
role in synthesizing heavier superheavy elements
whyHere: As a mid-series actinide with electrons filling further into the 5f subshell, berkelium is chemically similar to its lanthanide counterpart terbium, and its main scientific value today is as a bombardment target used to fuse together even heavier, more short-lived superheavy elements.
didYouKnow: A rare, carefully guarded sample of berkelium-249 was used as the target material that, when bombarded with calcium ions, led to the successful synthesis of tennessine (element 117) in 2010.
genZNote: Basically the periodic table's ammunition for making even heavier, weirder elements. Quietly essential to the whole superheavy-element project.
